questions.title: Capacitor timing circuit
questions.summary: Close S1 and time how long the voltmeter takes to pass zero: the capacitor charges through (P + R) until V_Y falls to half the supply, so t = (P + R)C ln 2. A graph of t against R gives b/a = P.

xlsx.desc: Six (R, t) pairs from combinations of 5 kΩ resistors. Plot t against R; b/a gives the resistance of P.

questions.title: Cooling of hot water
questions.summary: Plot the cooling curve from 80 °C to 70 °C and draw a tangent at 75 °C. Then linearise a datalogger dataset with ln(θ − 30) against t to find n and k, and plan an experiment linking k to the surface area of the water.

xlsx.desc: Thermometer readings every 20 s from 80 °C to 70 °C.
A practice version of datasetQ2b: θ every 30 s for 30 minutes. Plot ln(θ − 30) against t to find n and k.

questions.title: Conical pendulum
questions.summary: A bob is driven round a drawn circle of diameter D. With sin θ = D/2p, test T² = εp cos θ using two string lengths, find g = 4π²/ε, analyse a second data set (which turns out to be on the Moon), and plan a measurement of g with a pressure sensor.

xlsx.desc: Table 3.1 data. Compute T and cos θ, plot T² against cos θ and find ε (then g).

notes.text: With S2 closed the capacitor is shorted, so Y sits at X's potential and the voltmeter reads half the supply.
The moment of zero is when V_Y = E/2, i.e. after t = (P + R)C ln 2. That is why b/a works out to be P.
Repeat each timing (reaction time ≈ 0.2–0.3 s) and record t to 0.1 s.
Use six well-spread values: parallel/series combinations give 1.7 kΩ to 15 kΩ.
b/a = intercept ÷ gradient. Units: s ÷ (s kΩ⁻¹) = kΩ.
Check: b/a should match the resistance of P measured with the multimeter.
Start timing when the thermometer passes 80 °C and read every 20 s. Stir gently before each reading.
Draw a smooth curve through the points (not dot-to-dot), then a tangent touching it at 75 °C. Use a large triangle.
dθ/dt is negative (cooling). Give the sign and the unit °C s⁻¹.

notes.text: "One problem" should be specific: tangent judgement, the thermometer reading changing while you read it, or uneven temperature in the beaker.
Two marks: what m is (room temperature) + the reason (θ → m as t → ∞).
ln(θ − m) = ln n − kt, so plot ln(θ − 30) against t: gradient = −k and intercept = ln n.
n = e^(intercept), not the intercept itself. n has the unit °C; k has the unit s⁻¹.

If the relationship is valid, the</text></g><g class="ans" data-q="Q2"><text x="113.0" y="182.7" font-size="9" text-anchor="start" fill="#1550c8">graph is a straight line; α = gradient and β = y-intercept.
